title: One thing I know (John 9:25)
hookLine: a healed blind man can't win the argument, but he knows he was blind and now sees
carry: I was blind, now I see

lines: BORN BLIND, BEGGING BY THE ROAD.
cards: Ever argued with someone much cleverer than you? They have the vocabulary, the confidence, an answer for every point. You walk away thinking: I couldn't win that, but I still know what I know.
That's where a man in the Gospel of John ends up. Born blind, he begged by the road. Jesus spat on the ground, made mud, put it on his eyes and told him to go wash in the pool of Siloam.
He went, washed, and came back seeing. That should be the happy ending. Instead, an interrogation begins.

teach.h: THE NEIGHBORS ARGUE: IS IT HIM?
teach.b: Testimony is what a witness says about what they've seen. In John chapter nine, almost nobody is glad.
The neighbors argue about whether it's even the same man; some say he just looks like him, and he keeps saying: I am he. Then religious leaders question him.

It was the Sabbath, so some say the healer can't be from God, while others ask how a sinner could do such signs. They're divided. They call in his parents, who are afraid and say: he's of age, ask him.

They call him back and press him: we know this man is a sinner. His answer, in the King James Bible: "Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see."
He doesn't win the theology, and doesn't claim to. He just tells what happened.

The Greek word is martyria, and a witness is a martys, the root of our word martyr. At first it simply meant witness; later, as Christians died for what they testified, it came to mean one who dies for their faith.
He gets bolder under pressure and is put out. Then Jesus finds him, and he goes from calling Jesus a man, to a prophet, to worshipping him.

teach.h: WAS BLIND, BUT NOW I SEE.
teach.b: John tells it as a story about sight: the one who was blind sees more and more.

Much later, a former slave-ship captain named John Newton borrowed his words for a hymn: "I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see." A testimony doesn't need to be clever. It just needs to be true.

how: In many churches, people share their testimony, a short account of what they believe God has done in their lives, in services, small groups or baptisms; others keep it as a private record of answered prayer.

games.q: you were born blind and now you see. the authorities press you: we know the man who healed you is a sinner. what do you say?
o: argue theology with them point by point.
agree with them so you're not in trouble.
say you don't know about that, but you know you were blind and now see.
games.why: "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." he couldn't win the argument. he didn't need to.

practice: Let the questions about God or life you can't answer, the arguments you'd lose, be there.

Then look for one thing you know, not a doctrine but something that happened to you: a moment you were helped, a time you were forgiven, a night you somehow got through, a change you can't fully explain.
If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, just hold it.
